oneParagraphVerdict: This chapter clears the professional bar. It teaches one clean move: diagnose which villain is distorting the decision, then apply the matching WRAP repair. The prose is plain, memorable, and mechanism-heavy, with good boundaries around uncertainty and emergencies. The main weakness is quiz craftsmanship: several answers are fair but too easy to guess from mirrored wording and extreme distractors. Transfer is solid, though one later example feels more like a label drill than a consequential scenario.

items.rationale: Choice b is best supported because WRAP maps distinct moves to the four decision stages; choice c incorrectly delays it until after commitment.
The yes-or-no vendor framing is narrow framing, so adding real alternatives before further evidence review is the supported move.
Seeking disconfirming evidence directly counters confirmation bias after the team has begun favoring one plan.
The emotion lesson is to hear the attachment while gaining distance to judge what will matter later.
Mapping a wider range of plausible outcomes directly counters overconfidence in one neat forecast.
Steve Cole's logic supports funding parallel first passes so comparison can teach before commitment.
The outsider question creates distance from legacy attachment by asking what a fresh leader would do.
The four villains affect different stages, so different interruptions are needed rather than one final review.
WRAP improves the odds of a good decision without guaranteeing a good outcome under uncertainty.
